item.title: Texas's Democratic governor-elect wants to give every household $1,500
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
AUSTIN - GOP Gov. Greg Abbott and conservative state lawmakers tried to label incoming Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa a closet progressive, warning that she’ll turn the deeply red state socialist. But after Hinojosa’s historic upset win amid a blue wave that swept every state office, Texas’s first Latina governor-elect vowed during an interview with The Washington Post to avoid culture wars in favor of something Texas hasn’t seen in a generation: moderation. On a number of key issues facing her state - affordability, border security, data centers and school vouchers - Hinojosa is staking out what she calls populist positions that seem calibrated to appeal to voters at both ends of the political spectrum. That includes her pledge to work with President Donald Trump on immigration. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “I agree with President Trump that our border needs to be secure and people should not be coming here to cross into the country,” Hinojosa said at the state Capitol on Friday. “It’s a dangerous journey and I don’t think it will be fruitful for them.” In a Truth Social post Thursday about migrant caravans forming in Mexico, Trump referred to her as “the very liberal new governor of Texas.” Hinojosa, seated near a photo of the state’s last Democratic Gov. Ann Richards, said the Trump administration had not contacted her and she had not spoken to the president, “but I welcome that conversation.” “Trump and I won the same border communities: I won them this time, he won them last time” in 2024, said Hinojosa, who will preside over the country’s second-largest Latino population. Latino voters in places like her native Rio Grande Valley were instrumental in Democratic wins, including one county that swung away from Republicans by more than any other in the nation. Asked if she would end Operation Lone Star, the more than $11 billion-dollar state border security operation Abbott used emergency powers to launch in 2021, Hinojosa said she would review its legality. “It’s essential that we have strong partnership with Washington … to make sure our local border communities are safe,” she said. But she drew a distinction between border security and federal immigration enforcement in Texas’s interior. “The election was a referendum on how people are treated within our state, not outside of it, certainly not outside the country,” she said. After a migrant was fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Houston in July, and another ICE agent was indicted on federal assault charges there last month, Hinojosa stressed that federal agents securing the border was “very different from interior enforcement, which as we have all seen has been chaotic and dangerous and people died, people have been hurt. People are scared and angry and people’s rights are violated and that has to stop.” Last week, Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a Democrat, said he was directing police officers to limit their cooperation with ICE during traffic stops. That means he is challenging a policy imposed on the state’s largest city by Abbott, who had threatened to withhold state grant funding. Hinojosa said it was “wrong” for Abbott to require city police ”to hold people for ICE who were, for instance, reporting domestic violence assault. That is not good for public safety. That makes us less secure when people don’t feel that they can report crimes freely or face being handed over to ICE.” Hinojosa said she will not challenge Texas’s mostly Democratic municipal leaders if they block police from cooperating with ICE. But she also said she will not overturn a state law requiring sheriffs and counties that operate jails to comply with ICE. “I will always follow the law. The law is what it is. It’s up to the legislature if that’s going to get changed,” she said. The Texas governor has virtually unlimited emergency powers, which some GOP state lawmakers have said they fear Hinojosa will use to overturn conservative laws passed in recent years, including laws requiring people to use bathrooms that match their sex at birth, bans on abortion and gender transition medical care for minors. Hinojosa said those fears are unfounded. “I don’t see us trying to tackle culture wars. That was not the mandate we were given,” she said. “The mandate we were given was to deliver for Texans.” On day one, she said, she plans to declare a “high-cost emergency,” freeze electricity rates and suspend the 20-cent-per-gallon state gas and diesel tax. She also plans to immediately issue an emergency proclamation to the legislature to approve a measure that would send every Texas household $1,500. “That is the emergency that families are experiencing in their homes right now: They just can’t afford basics. They can’t pay their electric bills. They can’t afford to put food on the table. They can’t afford to see the doctor,” she said. Abbott had embraced Islamophobia, vowing to “ban sharia law,” blocking Muslim housing developments and designating the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the country’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, a terrorist group. Hinojosa said she would remove that designation. “We have to use public safety measures for public safety,” she said, dismissing what she called “nonsense happening with power that should be used for public safety, money that should use for public safety, that is not being used for safety.” She promised once she’s inaugurated Jan. 19 to declare a moratorium on data centers, but only those that have yet to receive state permits because “if they’ve already received state permits, I don’t have the power just to shut them down.” But Hinojosa acknowledged that “there are communities who are under the impression that their water will be shut off if there’s only enough water for either them or the data centers.” “I would intervene with all my power to stop that from happening,” she said, citing recent water shortages in Corpus Christi. “It can just never be the case that industry is prioritized over people for water that they drink and need to live.” Hinojosa, who like Abbott is Catholic, has said she personally opposes capital punishment. Texas has executed more than 600 death row inmates since the reinstatement of capital punishment in 1976, with an execution scheduled later this month. But unlike outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), who this month began the process of commuting the sentences of all 548 inmates on the state’s death row, Hinojosa said she would consider those on Texas’s death row “on a case-by-case basis and review and make a decision in accordance with the law.” Hinojosa voted against the state’s abortion ban but during her campaign she also released an ad in which she spoke about her decision to carry her first pregnancy to term even after genetic testing revealed a fetal anomaly. Since the abortion ban went into effect, Texas lawmakers increased funding to $200 million for more than 100 antiabortion pregnancy centers under a state program Hinojosa said she would review and potentially veto. “My understanding is a lot of that funding was not going to actually provide health care services for women. It should be,” she said. “I’m going to take a fine-tooth comb to that entire budget … If it is not serving Texans, not serving their health care needs, not serving families, then, yeah, I would veto that funding.” While Hinojosa voted against a state school voucher program and vowed on the campaign trail to fight it, she said that instead of executive action, she plans to work with the legislature to reshape the program, potentially using it to expand access to prekindergarten. “It’s going to all be one big negotiation,” she said. Hinojosa spoke out during her campaign against mid-decade redistricting her GOP colleagues forced through the legislature last summer despite a Democratic quorum break. But she said she doesn’t have to power to reverse it. ”That’s something that the legislature would have to pass a law to do,” she said. Republicans retained their majority in the state Senate, and some have suggested they may use Senate rules to strip the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor of her power to lead the senate, effectively blocking Democrats’ legislation and the governor’s priorities. But Hinojosa said Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin has been “working with her team to ensure that the voice of the voters is heard, and the voters voted for change.” Hinojosa was elected to the state legislature almost a decade ago, and said she has worked with Republicans on education and other issues, including a former GOP colleague she included on her transition team. She noted she’ll have help from two Democratic state senators - Nathan Johnson, who was elected attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt, the comptroller-elect. Walking the halls of the Capitol on Friday, Hinojosa shook hands with voters and children in tour groups, all of whom congratulated her. She visited the empty floors of the state House and Senate, pointing out the clear line of sight between them. “I am hearing very positive feedback from senators who are looking forward to working with me,” Hinojosa said. “I know how the legislative process works. I know these people. I know what’s important to them. And I know how to get things done here.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/14/texass-democratic-gov-elect-vows-trade-gop-culture-wars-moderation/

item.title: Silicon Valley is already plotting a comeback for ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
SAN FRANCISCO — A day after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, Silicon Valley is already anticipating his comeback. As a close ally of Donald Trump, regularly taking calls — even publicly — from the president, Huang became one of the most prominent and influential voices in Washington for the largely California-based tech industry, leaving a vacuum with his departure from one of the world’s most profitable companies that has become the backbone of the AI boom. But while national security hawks and tech skeptics in Washington prepare to haul him before Congress to bring further scrutiny of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, Silicon Valley leaders are mourning his swift exit and positing ways that he could return. The founder of defense tech giant Anduril, Palmer Luckey , and Perplexity AI CEO Aravind Srinivas have rushed to Huang’s defense, while SpaceXSI CEO Elon Musk has even floated the idea of hiring him. Five other tech industry insiders also told POLITICO they expect Huang to eventually return in a major way to leadership within Silicon Valley. Another three were not quite as confident, but indicated they wouldn’t be surprised if it happened. “It is inevitable, with all of the value that he’s created and his role commonly accepted as the godfather of AI, that he will have a second act,” said an executive at a prominent California startup who was granted anonymity to frankly discuss industry dynamics. “And that any number of hyperscalers and startups are tripping over themselves to reach out to him and bring him on, regardless of any transgressions.” Despite losing his lofty perch at Nvidia, Huang still has a net worth of roughly $145 billion , an ecosystem of connections in high places and a sterling entrepreneurial reputation within the industry, some noted. “That kind of influence doesn’t just disappear overnight,” said Joseph Hoefer, chief AI officer at the lobbying firm Monument Advocacy. “I wouldn’t confuse losing his position with losing his ability to shape what comes down the road.” A spokesperson for Huang did not respond to a request for comment on his future plans. Three of the people who spoke with POLITICO said it would be easier for Huang to start a new venture using his wealth of capital, rather than joining an already established company. The connection to allegations of espionage “would make it much harder for any public company to bring him on board in a leadership role,” said Scott Gerber, partner at the tech strategy consultancy Vrge. Others have started to seize on questions about the initial reports of Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, potentially undercutting any support for his ouster. Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), who will likely be the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, told POLITICO this week that he’s unsure whether Huang’s paramour was knowingly providing information to China based on briefings from U.S. intelligence officials. David Sacks, Trump’s former AI czar and a venture capitalist prominent on the tech right, highlighted reports that some in the U.S. intel community have similar doubts. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” he wrote in an X post . Recouping influence in Washington, however, may still be trickier than in Silicon Valley. Huang has been a commanding voice in advocating for looser restrictions on exports to China of advanced semiconductors — necessary for the development of artificial intelligence. That position is being called into question by lawmakers in Congress, given an initial Financial Times report that U.S. intelligence believed Huang was having an affair with a spy. “His standing in industry might be recoverable over time,” said Philip Reiner, CEO of the Institute for Security and Technology think tank in California and a former senior director at the National Security Council. “Rebuilding credibility in Washington on China policy is extremely challenging.” Even still, much of the cachet he built was specifically connected to Trump’s White House, meaning it would have an expiration date regardless, ahead of the 2028 election, others noted. “[M]uch of his political influence was tied to his relationship with the current administration, and that kind of access will be hard to rebuild once the political landscape shifts,” said Nu Wexler, a principal at Four Corners Public Affairs who advises tech companies on policy communications. This delicate position raises the stakes for an upcoming House hearing on the scandal, for which Huang has agreed to testify . “If he can come before Congress and own mistakes, but also explain them and still be a credible voice, that will go a long way towards opening the door for anything else that he would want to do in Washington and the private sector,” said Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation — a think tank funded by Big Tech companies like Amazon and Microsoft. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/13/silicon-valley-plots-jensen-huangs-comeback-01166322

item.title: Mary Peltola nears an Alaska Senate win as Democrats eye a 56th seat
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Campaign signs on October 30, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Democrat Mary Peltola has widened her lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's still-undecided U.S. Senate race, moving within striking distance of an outright victory that would give Democrats their 56th Senate seat following sweeping midterm gains. As of Saturday morning, Peltola had 49.8% of the vote, compared with Sullivan's 46.1%, a margin of more than 10,000 votes. The Associated Press reported 96% of votes counted, with Peltola receiving 138,240 votes to Sullivan's 127,828. The former congresswoman gained nearly 2,000 votes on Sullivan in the latest batch of ballots, strengthening her prospects of clearing the 50% threshold needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice voting tabulation. Peltola's campaign declared victory Friday, insisting the Republican incumbent could no longer overcome her advantage. "There is no mathematical path for Sullivan to win this race," the campaign said in a statement posted on X. "When the remaining votes are counted, Mary will decisively be elected as Alaska’s next United States Senator," the statement read. Campaign manager Cheryl Bruce echoed that confidence in a statement to Newsweek. "As more ballots get counted, it’s clear that Mary’s victory is all but guaranteed, and Alaskans have resoundingly rejected Dan Sullivan’s D.C. self dealing," Bruce said. "Mary won today’s ballot drop by a decisive margin, and remaining votes from Anchorage, Juneau, and rural Alaska will continue to break for Mary, continuing her momentum to the United States Senate. "Alaskans are ready for a senator who fights to lower costs and takes on D.C. corruption, and when every vote is counted, Mary will deliver for Alaska," Bruce said. Sullivan's campaign, however, declined to concede. "We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we’ll see what happens from there," campaign spokesman Nate Adams told The New York Times on Friday. The race remained uncalled Saturday, with outstanding ballots potentially determining whether Peltola secures an outright majority or must prevail through ranked-choice voting. Under Alaska's system, if no candidate receives more than 50% of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidates are eliminated and their supporters' subsequent preferences redistributed until a winner emerges. Two minor candidates, Republican Gerald Heikes and unaffiliated Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., have collectively captured roughly 4% of the vote. Democrats recruited both candidates in an effort to weaken the incumbent's support, according to The New York Times. The Trump administration previously challenged the election over the presence of another candidate named Sullivan, arguing potential voter confusion, but the lawsuit was dismissed. Alaska has until Nov. 18 to complete its vote count, with ranked-choice tabulation to follow if necessary. A Peltola victory would represent another significant Democratic pickup in a midterm election that has already delivered the party 55 Senate seats, its largest majority since the early Obama administration. Peltola, who campaigned on "fish, family, and freedom," would become the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win an Alaska Senate seat in nearly two decades. Her potential victory would also underscore Republican difficulties in a state President Donald Trump carried by approximately 14 percentage points in 2024, amid voter concerns over high prices, the administration's war in Iran, and tariffs affecting Alaska's economy. In another major Democratic victory in Alaska, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, has won the state's gubernatorial election, defeating three Republican opponents in a four-way contest, according to Decision Desk HQ. Kreiss-Tomkins will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, becoming Alaska's youngest governor and the first Democrat elected to the office in more than two decades. His victory came after national political organizations poured millions into the contest, with Democrats benefiting from a divided Republican field despite Trump's endorsement of Bernadette Wilson. Meanwhile, Alaska's U.S. House race remains uncalled, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich III leading in a contest expected to proceed to ranked-choice tabulation. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.This article originally appeared on Newsmax at https://www.newsmax.com/newsfront/alaska-mary-peltola-dan-sullivan/2026/11/14/id/1276300

item.title: After 26 years, the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nearly all measles cases have been in people who had not received the highly effective measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. - Jayla Whitfield-Anderson/Reuters Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles had been considered “eliminated” as a continually transmitting illness in the United States since 2000 – but not anymore. An independent commission of experts that reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The decision was widely expected after years of falling vaccination levels and surging case counts, but it’s still a black mark on the nation’s public health policy. The international committee that determines countries’ measles elimination status considers an infection to be endemic, or regularly occurring, if infections caused by the same strain are passed from person to person for at least a year within the same country. To determine this, the committee members look at the genetic code of viruses sampled from patients. Every time a virus copies itself, it makes tiny changes in its genetic code. By studying the genomes of different viruses in an outbreak, scientists can determine how closely the infections may be related and whether they are likely to have been part of the same chains of transmission. In August, scientists with Utah’s public health laboratory published a preprint study showing that the same strain of measles had been circulating in the state for more than a year, accounting for more than 95% of cases there. It traveled from the southwest part of the state to central Utah, ultimately causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026. There have also been sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York, as well as other states. It’s not clear what data the committee relied on to make its decision, but it wasn’t exactly a tough call, said Dr. Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan in Canada and Editor-in-Chief of the journal Vaccine. The Utah data alone would have been enough to make the case, she said. The US has logged record numbers of measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths for the past two years, even as some members of the Trump administration – including President Donald Trump – have cast doubt on the safety and effectiveness of the vaccines that prevent it. “Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system. It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is so effective that two doses cut an exposed person’s chances of getting sick by 97% compared with someone who is unvaccinated. Since 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country has still some outbreaks every year. These were touched off by sick travelers who brought the virus into the country. Because of community protection maintained by high vaccination rates, these outbreaks were usually small and short-lived. In 2025 and 2026 , however, the virus found more families and communities that were unvaccinated, leaving them vulnerable to infection. More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year – the highest number since 1991. Most are linked to the 43 new outbreaks this year, but more than 1,000 cases are linked to outbreaks that began last year. Nearly all of this year’s cases have been in people who had not received the MMR vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported cases, according to the CDC , and at least 10 people have died after catching measles, according to state reports. ‘Measles is back’ The declaration is a humbling moment for a nation that played a leading role in ridding the world of smallpox – the only human disease to have ever been wiped out worldwide – and worked for decades to drive measles offshore. “This is just so devastating and so sad that we are where we are today,” said Dr. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an infectious disease epidemiologist at Columbia University Irvine Medical Center in New York. “This just kind of points towards the direction of really reversing a generation of public health progress.” But it also means people who are too young to be vaccinated against measles or who have lowered immune function because of organ transplants or cancer or other conditions are at higher risk in areas with outbreaks than they were just two years ago. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported measles cases this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. - Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Most people who get measles will recover after having a fever and a rash and feeling generally miserable for several days, said Dr. William Moss, a professor and measles expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But that doesn’t mean the infection is benign, he said. Measles can also wipe out a person’s immune memory. The immune system forgets which infections it’s fought off before, leaving the person vulnerable to secondary threats like pneumonia or diarrhea. If a pregnant woman catches measles, she can pass it to her baby in the womb, and the baby will be born with measles, putting its life at risk. In rare cases, people who’ve had measles can develop serious neurologic complications, sometimes years after the original infection. The most serious is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is progressive and fatal. All of these complications can be prevented by vaccination. The United States losing its measles elimination status is “incredibly embarrassing,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston. But, he said, it’s a signal of an more important message: “Basically, measles is back.” “Whether or not we’ve officially lost our elimination status to me is much less important than, basically, measles is here. It’s pervasive, and vaccination rates are down across the country, and I don’t see us getting back to normal anytime soon,” he added. Could the US regain its elimination status? Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to science. A single infected person typically spreads it to 12 to 18 others. The virus is airborne and can float in a room for hours after a sick person leaves it. Soon after the measles vaccine was deployed in the early 1960s, public health experts realized that if enough people in an area were vaccinated, the protection from the shot could stop the spread of the virus. The US set its first goal to eliminate measles transmission in 1978. Measles is one of the 30 diseases targeted for elimination by 2030 by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO. In 2016, PAHO and the World Health Organization declared the 35 countries in the Americas region to be free of ongoing measles transmission. That designation was lost last year, however, when Canada’s elimination status ended after a lengthy outbreak that spanned several provinces. Mexico, which has had several large measles outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing its elimination status. Moss said that since the US has lost its measles elimination status, it has to be on the path to regaining it. “That’s not easy, particularly in the current environment with diminished public trust in vaccines, the increasing nonmedical exemptions that we’re seeing in schools, and declines in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination among our kindergarten students, and the undermining of vaccine policy,” Moss said. “So it’s not going to be a trivial task for the United States to regain its measles elimination status.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/13/health/us-measles-elimination-status

item.title: Trump says the Iran war is 'effectively over.' The U.S. is still spending millions.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump this week declared the war in Iran “effectively over” militarily and “won” by the U.S. But he did so as American taxpayers are footing the bill for billions of dollars in operational costs to keep the country’s troops at the ready overseas. The war is no longer making top headlines, and firing between the U.S. and Iran is not taking place on a daily basis. Yet the U.S. has a large presense in the region and is effectively in a war posture, despite the president's remarks, which come after a midterm shellacking for his party driven in part by voter unhappiness over the war. “We won. Now the question is when we want to end. We must have a total victory. Not a 93 percent victory. It's going to be total,” Trump said Wednesday in remarks during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. A few days prior in a surprise visit to the White House briefing room, Trump declared: “Iran militarily is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo.” Despite Trump's remarks, the U.S. is spending millions on the Iran conflict. The total cost of the fight as of Oct. 16 is estimated at $47.1 billion, including $38 billion accrued from when the war began on Feb. 28 up until the start of August, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO). That means another $9 billion was added over the last three months or so, a relatively quiet period that underscores the costs to taxpayers. During that timeframe, the U.S. military reportedly only carrying out a handful of defensive strikes against the regime after it all but depleted its stockpiles of advanced munitions. That's $2 billion to $3 billion per month in continuing costs, meaning the war is approaching a $50 billion price tag, according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank. She warned that those costs could escalate if there is an increase in fighting. “The war is not over,” Yacoubian told The Hill. “If there is a spike in conflict, war costs will also spike.” Trump this week indicated it’s unlikely he will order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the war continue positively. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday. “The answer is, highly unlikely ‌it's going to be necessary.” Talks between the two sides are taking place but appear shaky, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Wednesday accusing the U.S. of threatening to attack his country with America’s “mother of all bombs,” its largest non-nuclear weapon even as the U.S. pursues a peace deal. The big cost for the U.S. comes from maintaining a naval blockade on Iran in the Strait of Hormuz. Yacoubian described this as “a 24-7 operation that entails all sorts of costs related to diverting some ships, intercepting others, protecting friendly ones, not to mention U.S. force protection.” “All of these elements have costs associated which is why the blockade could be difficult to sustain over an extended period,” she added. Washington’s naval blockade of Iranian ports has now lasted more than 100 days, an undertaking that has cost considerable sums. In the first week of November, the U.S. military maintained two aircraft carriers, 11 destroyers and a cruiser in the Arabian Sea, along with two destroyers in the Red Sea. Another three destroyers are operating under the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean Sea, according to the Institute for National Security Studies. Alongside the blockade - which requires American ships to burn through fuel, food and other critical supplies for tens of thousands of service members - the United States has carried out limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets should Tehran fire upon its aircraft or vessels. The most recent such incident fell on Nov. 2, when U.S. warplanes struck an anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island and another island in the Strait of Hormuz after Tehran fired a missile at an American aircraft. Outside the everyday costs to fuel America’s war machine in the Middle East, the Pentagon has suffered more than $65 billion in estimated costs to repair or replace U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks - something that hasn’t been factored into CBO estimates, according to Yacoubian. The Trump administration is requesting up to $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the Iran war and to pay for new weapons and personnel. The president as of late has insisted U.S. allies in the Middle East will “pay” America’s bill for the conflict. “Those countries that we've protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we've had for the war,” the president said in an interview with CBS News that aired Sunday. Outside of direct cost to the U.S. govenment, the continued chokehold of the Strait of Hormuz has kept fuel costs and the prices of other goods heightened for U.S. consumers, an issue that Republican lawmakers admit torpedoed their chances to keep control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. Case in point, America’s households are expected to face higher fuel costs this winter, with heating costs projected to average $1,002 across all fuels, up 7.1 percent from last winter, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association released this week. Those who rely primarily on heating oil - more than 4 million households - will pay some $2,977 this winter, up roughly 70 percent from last year. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. item.title: U.S. floated idea of Ukraine surrendering territory for NATO membership, Zelensky says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Olena Harmash KYIV, Nov 14 (Reuters) - US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu ‌Dhabi. This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskiy ‌said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" he said. "That is why I believe NATO ​is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation." Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia's full-blown invasion in 2022. Zelenskiy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian ‌army and funds to rebuild, he would put the ⁠question to a national referendum. 'THIS WAR MUST BE ENDED FIRST' Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskiy dismissed Russia's call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the ⁠specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. "We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first," he said. Zelenskiy also dismissed Putin's suggestion for ​a ​local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, ​saying it reflected Moscow's inability to take the city by ‌force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added. "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way," he said. Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskiy said. Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war. LARGE PRISONER EXCHANGE AGREED The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed ‌to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskiy said. The final ​numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added. US peace envoys Steve Witkoff ​and Jared Kushner had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with ​Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskiy said, but there was no news of any progress after ‌their talks. "Putin personally does not support a ceasefire," he said. Zelenskiy ​met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in ​Ireland after their talks in Moscow. He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks. In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine's largest financial and ​military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials ‌but did not sit at the table with Russia. At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe's team for any ​Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as ​EU officials. (Reporting by Olena Harmash; Editing by Daniel Flynn and Gareth Jones) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/us-floated-idea-ukraine-ceding-122531169.html

item.title: Microsoft says AI didn’t break Outlook — its own network upgrade did
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Millions of office workers got an unplanned break from email Thursday. Their bosses' favorite new AI tool got one too. A Microsoft ( MSFT ) outage that began midday Thursday knocked out Outlook and other workplace apps worldwide, with Downdetector logging reports from 74 countries within about an hour. By Friday, Microsoft said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress." The damage reached Microsoft's AI. Copilot couldn't access users' email, files, or calendars, and the Microsoft connectors for OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) Claude broke too. Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its Microsoft 365 apps. Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Yahoo Finance What it means for you Your email isn't lost. Microsoft stretched its email timeout to 48 hours , so messages sent to you keep trying to deliver instead of bouncing back. There isn't much to fix on your end. Resetting your password or reinstalling Outlook won't help, though desktop Outlook may still show mail it already downloaded. If your company pays for Microsoft 365, it may be owed money. Microsoft promises 99.9% uptime , about 43 minutes of downtime a month, with credits of 25% to 100% of the monthly fee when it falls short. Your IT department has to file the claim. Not the first time Microsoft is hard to replace, which is usually good news for its shareholders. Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, whose fund owns Microsoft stock, said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that Microsoft is "the gateway to how people interact with the basic workflows of a desk worker," which makes it "a much more difficult position to dislodge." This week showed the other side of that. Microsoft has blamed its own changes or maintenance for Microsoft 365 disruptions in at least six months this year, from a nearly 10-hour outage in January to a spam-filter update that bounced real email earlier this month. Australia's home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said Microsoft believes it's dealing with "an update that has gone awry," much like the 2024 CrowdStrike meltdown. Microsoft, The Register, BleepingComputer, Petri, Yahoo Finance Have you tried turning it off and on again? Microsoft reached for the oldest fix in the help desk manual, saying Thursday it was "restarting affected servers to return them to service." It didn’t stick. Servers that came back went down again once traffic returned. On Friday, Microsoft traced the outage to a problem from “an earlier network capacity upgrade” that surfaced after a recent network change, and said it was “deeply sorry for the disruption.” Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Yahoo Finance What we know about the layoffs The outage comes as Microsoft trims its workforce while spending heavily on AI. It offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees in October, and those who accept leave Dec. 31. CEO Satya Nadella said last year that AI writes "maybe 20%, 30%" of Microsoft's code . Microsoft says AI wasn’t the culprit. It called the outage “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents” in a post on X . In a statement to Yahoo Finance, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the company regrets “the impact these outages had on those who depend on us” and that “our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.” He didn’t address questions about staffing. Chris Versace, chief investment officer at Tematica Research, put the lesson simply: "The outage and how it hobbled many businesses and other enterprises is a reminder about the need for redundancies." Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com . item.title: Police find credible bomb threat at Illinois plant and urge evacuations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Authorities are investigating a "credible" threat at a plant in Peoria, Illinois, after a device was discovered at the facility Friday night and later rendered safe by bomb technicians. No additional devices were found and the evacuation order within a one-mile blast radius of the BioUrja Renewables facility has been lifted after investigators searched the facility for hours, Peoria police said Saturday. Police determined at about 6:45 p.m. local time Friday that a package at the facility was a credible threat and established a one-mile blast radius, officials said. 25News - PHOTO: Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon speaks at a press conference on Nov. 14, 2026, in Peoria, Ill. Bomb technicians "rendered the package safe" at about 9:12 p.m. local time, according to police. A law enforcement source told ABC News Saturday the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and FBI are leading an investigation, and it is criminal in nature. ATF special agents were on the scene clearing the building, the source said. Asked about the device found Friday night, Police Chief Brad Dixon said he would not discuss that further, explaining that it is "part of the criminal investigation." Dixon said he could not say "what type of device it was." Officials had said they were not treating the incident as a hoax. "When a bomb threat comes in, typically, it's not legitimate, and they're doing it to cause an evacuation of a building or something like that," Dixon said at a press conference late Friday. "This is not the case here. We found a credible package that we deem to be a threat. This is ... this is not. We're not considering this a hoax." Authorities had closed most streets in the area Friday night and urged the public to avoid the one-mile radius around the facility until further notice. Approximately 60 to 80 people were at the designated "shelter place" -- a high school -- Dixon said earlier. Officials conducted door-to-door notifications in the entire radius. Asked if the incident was being investigated as a terrorist threat, Dixon said that officials would not comment on the criminal investigation as it is "active" and "open." The police chief explained the search was difficult due to the facility's size, describing it as large as 44 1/2 football fields. 25News - PHOTO: Law enforcement vehicles are shown at the scene after a bomb was found at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Ill., on Nov. 13, 2026. Chris Amon of the ATF Chicago Field Division said that the agency "and our partners remain committed to finding the person or persons responsible for this criminal act and ensuring that they are held fully accountable for their actions." “To date, our office has provided investigative bomb technician and intelligence resources toward this collective effort," Ryan Presley, special agent-in-charge of the FBI Springfield Field Office, said. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said on social media he was "actively monitoring the bomb threat in Peoria, and I have directed the Illinois State Police to coordinate with local authorities." He urged residents to follow directions from police and stay away from the evacuated area. Country music singer Jon Pardi's concert in Peoria was also canceled because of its proximity to the bomb threat. Pardi posted a message to his Instagram followers Friday night, saying, "Peoria, we're disappointed that we won't get to spend tonight with you, but the safety of our fans, our team and the community is always the priority. At the discretion of the Chief of Police, tonight's concert has been canceled due to an active local safety concern. Thank you for your understanding, and stay safe." -ABC News' Luke Barr contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/US/peoria-police-urge-evacuations-after-reported-bomb-threat/story?id=138137440

item.title: Duffy says contractor work disrupted communications leading to grounded flights
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, and Rebecca Gay, FAA Acting Chief Technology Officer, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner) AP Photo/Tom Brenner Airlines canceled thousands more flights Saturday as they recovered from Friday’s nationwide ground stop, but the FAA said schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday. More than 5,000 U.S. flights had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware , already past the top of the 4,000 to 5,000 that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted. Flight-tracking app Flighty said the outage has now caused more cancellations than the 2024 CrowdStrike software failure. “I do think the worst is behind us,” Bedford said, and he apologized to travelers. The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. About 12,000 flights couldn’t be completed, Bedford said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began while L3Harris Technologies, which runs the network, was doing routine work to switch lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. A router involved in the work flooded the rest of the system, disrupting communications with airplanes and radar. Duffy said officials are working to determine “whether we had incompetence” by the contractor or a faulty router. “Until I can build” a new network, he said, “I’m stuck with L3Harris.” Bedford said the review will determine whether the router was installed or configured incorrectly, or was simply defective. In a statement to Yahoo News, L3Harris said it is “supporting the FAA in its investigation” and “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The company did not address Duffy’s criticism or say what went wrong. Asked why the work was done on a Friday afternoon, Duffy said work at small, remote sites is done during the day because it isn’t expected to affect the wider system. “There’ll be a reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said. Bedford said maintenance on the network is logged on paper, so officials had to search through paper records to figure out who was working where. Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told Yahoo News that communications with some planes were disrupted during the outage and that controllers moved flights to working frequencies. Asked whether work like Friday’s should be done during the day, he said, “If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there’s the fewest airplanes in the sky.” The network’s problems aren’t new. A 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review called it obsolete, CBS News reported . In 2009, a technician for L3Harris’ predecessor, Harris Corp., misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 air traffic facilities, according to a Transportation Department inspector general review . Duffy is pressing Congress for more money to replace the system. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy has said he wants $50 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. Bedford said the router swap was routine maintenance, not part of that modernization effort. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign Saturday. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation . Travelers whose flights were canceled are owed a refund if they choose not to fly, and most major airlines are offering travel waivers. Airlines’ promises of hotels and meals generally cover only disruptions within their control, which doesn’t include an FAA ground stop. item.title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Starship rocket launched successfully on Friday [Getty Images] SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth. The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower. But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea. The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday. This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs. The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time on Friday. The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned. A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding. The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames [Reuters] During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely." The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet. The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off. SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the "chopsticks". Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space. If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean. A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon [SpaceX] Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX. In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster. Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch. But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society. "Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said. "One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate." After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa. The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline. What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next? Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface. But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown. Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule. Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage. Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended. But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida. Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027. Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030. This article originally appeared on BBC at https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ckregdgnl0xpo?xtor=AL-72-%5Bpartner%5D-%5Byahoo.north.america%5D-%5Bheadline%5D-%5Bnews%5D-%5Bbizdev%5D-%5Bisapi%5D
